Title: People-Centred Medical Image Analysis
Text:
People-Centred Medical Image Analysis
Zheng Zhanga, Milad Masroora, Cuong Nguyena, Tahir Hassanc, Yuanhong
Chene, David Rosewarneb, Kevin Wellsa, Thanh-Toan Dod,
Gustavo Carneiroa
aCVSSP, PAI, University of Surrey, UK
bRoyal Wolverhampton Hospitals NHS Trust, UK
cSouthampton Solent University, UK
dDepartment of Data Science and AI, Monash University, Australia
eAIML, Adelaide University, Australia
Abstract
Recent advances in data-centric medical AI have produced highly accurate
diagnostic systems, but the emphasis on data curation and performance met-
rics has not translated into widespread clinical adoption.
We conjecture
that this limited uptake stems from insufficient attention dedicated to the
optimisation of fair performance across diverse patient populations and to
workflow integration: performance biases can create regulatory barriers, and
poorly integrated automation can disrupt clinical routines, degrade the qual-
ity of human-AI collaboration, and reduce clinicians’ willingness to adopt
AI tools. Prior work on workflow integration (e.g., Learning to Defer (L2D)
and Learning to Complement (L2C)) and AI fairness has typically examined
these challenges in isolation, overlooking their natural interdependence and
the practical constraints of clinical environments, such as restricted clinician
availability. We propose People-Centred Medical Image Analysis (PecMan),
a human-AI framework that jointly optimises fairness, diagnostic accuracy,
and workflow effectiveness through a dynamic gating mechanism that assigns
cases to AI, clinicians, or both under clinician workload constraints. We also
introduce the Fairness and Human-Centred AI (FairHAI) benchmark for
evaluating trade-offs between accuracy, fairness, and clinician workload. Ex-
periments using this benchmark show that PecMan consistently outperforms
existing methods, paving the way for more trustworthy and clinically viable
AI systems. Code will be available upon paper acceptance.

1. Introduction
The rapid advancements in medical image analysis have led to highly ac-
curate data-centric medical AI models that are increasingly being integrated
into clinical practice [1]. These developments are particularly impactful in ra-
diology, where the volume of medical imaging far exceeds the capacity of the
available workforce [2]. By reliably assisting with diagnostic tasks, AI has the
potential to enhance diagnostic workflows by improving efficiency, reliability,
and consistency, thereby supporting high-quality patient care [3]. Despite
these promising advancements, hesitancy persists among clinicians [4] and
patients [5], compounded by unresolved regulatory challenges [6]. In par-
ticular, ensuring equitable performance across diverse populations is widely
recognised as both an ethical obligation and a regulatory requirement [6].
These challenges partly explain why healthcare does not rank among the top
ten industries hiring for AI roles in 20241. This reluctance reflects deeper
concerns about limited stakeholder engagement, particularly clinicians [7],
patients [8], and regulatory agencies [9], in shaping how AI systems are de-
signed, validated, and integrated into practice, alongside persistent questions
about accuracy for non-majoritarian groups, workflow impact, and compli-
ance with ethical and regulatory standards.
For patients and regulatory agencies, a primary concern is whether AI
models can be personalised to account for individual variations [10]. Ex-
isting models, even those with high overall accuracy, may underperform for
specific demographic groups due to biases in the training data or learning
algorithm [11, 12].
These concerns have been studied by the field of AI
fairness, which aims to ensure equitable model performance across diverse
patient populations [13].
Clinicians and healthcare settings are primarily
concerned with improving diagnostic performance while reducing workload,
but the cost-effectiveness of AI systems in routine practice remains unproven,
a challenge that Learning to Defer (L2D) [14] and Learning to Complement
(L2C) [15] aim to address by enabling more effective human-AI collabora-
tion. In particular, L2D models determine whether a case should be handled
by AI or deferred to a clinician, while L2C methods combine the human and
AI predictions. Even though both L2D and L2C aim to maximise diagnostic
accuracy, only L2D manages the cost of human involvement.

Although AI fairness, L2D, and L2C all aim to improve AI-assisted med-
ical decision-making, they have traditionally been studied in isolation. AI
fairness typically seeks to reduce disparities in model performance across pa-
tient groups [16], L2D focuses on optimising how responsibility is shared be-
tween clinicians and AI systems to ensure efficient collaboration [14], and L2C
aims to enhance joint prediction by leveraging the complementary strengths
of humans and machines [15]. Some efforts have explored the intersection
of fairness and L2D. For instance, Madras et al. [14] proposed a regulariser
to enforce equal false positive and false negative rates across patient cohorts
within an L2D framework. However, their approach assumes prior knowl-
edge of patient group membership for testing and does not incorporate L2C.
This assumption limits applicability in real-world settings, where such group
information may not be readily available, and overlooking L2C can lead to
suboptimal decision-making. In this work, we argue that (1) we should not
assume that prior knowledge of patient group membership is available for
testing, and (2) fairness, L2D, and L2C are fundamentally interconnected:
fairness influences AI reliability, which directly impacts both delegation (L2D)
and cooperation (L2C) decisions. Ignoring their interplay risks overlooking
important trade-offs and failing to meet the needs of both patients and clini-
cians.
To address this gap, we propose People-Centred Medical Image Analysis
(PecMan), a unified framework, depicted in Fig. 1, that integrates AI fair-
ness, L2D and L2C to enhance diagnosis accuracy, patient equity and clinical
3


efficacy without assuming any prior knowledge of patient group member-
ship during testing. PecMan optimises multiple objectives simultaneously,
namely: maximising overall and group-specific accuracy and minimising per-
formance disparities between patient groups under specific constraints for
clinician workload. We also propose the Fairness and Human-Centred AI
(FairHAI) benchmark, the first to jointly evaluate accuracy, fairness, and
clinician workload, addressing a gap where no such benchmarks currently
exist. To summarise, our key contributions include:
• The PecMan framework that jointly addresses AI fairness, human-AI
cooperation (through integrated L2D and L2C strategies), clinician
workload reduction, and improvements in both overall and cohort-
specific diagnostic accuracy by training multiple group-specific AI mod-
els and combining them within a unified decision-making mechanism
that dynamically allocates cases to AI, clinicians, or collaborative anal-
ysis;
• The new FairHAI benchmark for evaluating AI fairness and human-AI
cooperation, leveraging public medical imaging datasets.
Experimental results on the proposed FairHAI benchmark demonstrate that
PecMan outperforms existing methods that consider AI fairness, L2D and
L2C in isolation, leading to a more equitable, accurate, and effective AI-
assisted radiology workflow.
2. Literature Review
This paper goes beyond classification accuracy to address the needs of key
stakeholders in medical AI (i.e., clinicians, healthcare settings, patients, and
regulatory agencies) by aligning system design with their workflows and pri-
orities to foster trust, usability, and clinical effectiveness. For clinicians and
healthcare providers, we advocate for AI as an assistive tool that enhances
human-centred decision-making rather than replacing it [3]. For patients and
regulators, we tackle critical challenges of fairness and diagnostic reliability
to ensure equitable and effective care delivery [17]. However, current method-
ologies often treat fairness and human-AI cooperation as separate objectives,
overlooking their interdependence. Addressing this gap motivates our devel-
opment of PecMan, a unified framework that jointly optimises fairness and
human-AI collaboration.
4


2.1. Fairness in Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Fairness in AI has become a central concern in healthcare due to the
growing body of evidence showing that machine learning models can prop-
agate or amplify biases related to race, gender, age, and other sensitive at-
tributes [16, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. Ensuring fair performance
across diverse populations is recognised as an ethical and regulatory imper-
ative given that algorithmic biases can undermine trust in AI systems [27]
and exacerbate health disparities, particularly for under-represented popula-
tions [28, 29].
Bias mitigation strategies can be broadly categorised into pre-processing,
in-processing, and post-processing techniques, as follows:
1. Pre-processing approaches (e.g., SMOTE [30]) re-balance datasets prior
to training.
2. Post-processing methods (e.g., equalised odds [31]) adjust outputs after
training.
3. In-processing methods directly modify the training to reduce bias while
maintaining performance [24, 32, 33, 34].
Among these, in-processing methods tend to show superior results, so we
focus on these methods below. For instance, adversarial training [24, 32]
has been widely used to minimise a model’s ability to predict sensitive at-
tributes, though often at the cost of reduced accuracy [33, 34]. Another no-
table in-processing method is Group Distributionally Robust Optimisation
(GroupDRO) [35] that focuses on minimising worst-case performance across
demographic groups. Although GroupDRO ensures fairness across underper-
forming groups, it may reduce overall model performance [16]. Furthermore,
domain generalization methods such as SWAD [36] improve robustness by
finding flatter loss minima, but may inadvertently prioritise majority groups
and fail to optimise for group fairness. Other in-processing approaches like
representation disentanglement aim to isolate sensitive attributes from task-
relevant features [37, 38], though they struggle with complex, multi-source
biases. More recent methods have explicitly addressed group fairness while
preserving accuracy.
FairSeg [39] introduces Fair Error-Bound Scaling to
rebalance loss across groups.
FairCLIP [40] applies optimal transport to
align demographic distributions in vision-language models. FairVision [41]
incorporates Fair Identity Scaling to improve fairness in multimodal medical
imaging. Despite their innovation, these methods rely on a single model, of-
ten facing the challenging trade-off between group fairness and global perfor-
5


mance. In contrast, the AI fairness part of our approach leverages multiple
cohort-specific AI models to optimise each subgroup independently, effec-
tively balancing fairness and accuracy through an effective gating mecha-
nism.
2.2. Human-AI Cooperation
Traditional machine learning systems are typically optimised without con-
sidering how they interact with human users [42, 43, 44]. Although method-
ologically sound, this assumption often breaks down in practice due to the
complexity of real human-AI dynamics. Recent research highlights the need
for AI systems that not only assist but also interact effectively with human
experts [45], with factors such as model confidence [46, 47] and explainabil-
ity [48, 49] playing an important role in shaping that interaction. Crucially,
this interaction must be bidirectional: while AI influences human decisions,
human behaviours and judgments also shape AI outcomes. This duality is
the core of human-AI cooperative classification (HAI-CC) [50, 51, 52, 53, 15],
where decisions can be made in one of three ways:
1. AI predicts alone.
2. AI defers decisions to human experts.
3. AI makes a joint decision with human experts.
Below, we explain the main HAI-CC approaches being studied in the litera-
ture, relating them to these three options.
Learning to Defer (L2D). L2D methods primarily focus on options (1) and
(2), where either the AI or the human makes the final decision. These ap-
proaches aim to jointly learn a predictor and a rejector, enabling the AI to
defer decisions to humans when it is uncertain [14, 54, 55, 56, 57]. Early work
drew on rejection learning [58], and subsequent research developed surrogate
loss functions that are consistent with the Bayes-optimal classifier obtained
in the case of 0-1 loss [55, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69]. Other
advancements include score-based triage [60] and differentiable triage [61],
which assign decisions based on estimated human versus model errors. How-
ever, one common limitation of L2D-based methods is the reliance on the
single-expert setting, overlooking the more complex environments with the
availability of multiple experts. Hence, recent research in L2D has shifted the
focus to the multiple-expert setting [70, 56, 71, 54, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76]. De-
spite such an extensive research, current L2D-based learning methods have
6


not been designed to enable AI models and human experts to jointly produce
a final classification. To address this gap, “learning to complement” methods
have been introduced as explained below.
Learning to Complement (L2C). L2C methods explore scenarios where AI
and humans combine their predictions to maximise the expected utility of
the human-AI decision [15, 77, 78, 79, 50, 80] (options 1 and 3). Techniques
include: 1) confusion-matrix-based fusion [78]; 2) Bayesian modeling of joint
predictions [77]; and leveraging perceptual differences [79] to improve perfor-
mance through hybrid systems. These methods show that human-AI coop-
eration can outperform either party alone. However, unlike L2D approaches,
most L2C methods do not account for the cost of collaboration (e.g., time,
effort, annotation burden), limiting practical adoption.
Learning to Defer and to Complement (L2D + L2C). A small number of
recent works explore both L2D and L2C jointly. Notably, LECODU [81] in-
tegrates deferral and cooperation within a unified learning framework, mark-
ing an important step toward more comprehensive human-AI cooperative
systems. Nevertheless, this approach did not consider the AI fairness aspect,
like we do in PecMan.
2.3. Learning to Defer and AI Fairness
The interplay between fairness and L2D has been studied by Madras
et al.[14] with the incorporation of a fairness regulariser (e.g., equalised
false positives and false negatives across patient cohorts) into L2D optimi-
sation. However, their approach requires prior knowledge of demographic
group membership during testing and does not incorporate L2C. These limi-
tations reduce applicability in real-world settings where group attributes are
not guaranteed to be available, and where optimal performance may rely on
joint decisions rather than deferral alone. In contrast, our work explicitly
models the interdependence between fairness, L2D, and L2C and does not
assume the knowledge of demographic group membership for testing. By
doing so, we seek to advance people-centred medical AI systems that are not
only accurate and fair but also cooperative and adaptive to diverse clinical
contexts in real-world scenarios.
2.4. Fairness and HAI-CC Benchmarks
Current benchmarks for HAI-CC, L2D, and L2C remain fragmented.
Early L2D work introduced small-scale benchmarks using vision datasets
7


(e.g., CIFAR), paired with simulated experts or cost-sensitive rejection mod-
els [14, 59], and later studies extended these evaluations to multiple-expert
settings [54]. L2C methods similarly assess complementarity on standard
image classification datasets, often relying on synthetic human error models
or retrospective clinician labels to estimate collaborative gains [77, 78]. Al-
though these resources provide insight into isolated aspects of collaboration,
such as deferral quality or fusion benefits, they do not evaluate fairness or
multi-rater variability.
In contrast, fairness in medical imaging has been supported by more
structured benchmark resources. Early analyses of hidden stratification and
demographic performance gaps highlighted the need for fairness-aware evalu-
ation in clinical AI [12, 28]. More recent frameworks such as MEDFAIR [16]
provide standardised protocols across multiple medical imaging modalities,
enabling consistent measurement of group-specific disparities. Task-specific
fairness suites, including FairVision [82] for ophthalmology and FairSeg [39]
for segmentation, extend these ideas by incorporating fairness-aware metrics.
However, these fairness benchmarks do not consider human-AI collaboration,
deferral behaviour, or workflow-related constraints, leaving fairness evalua-
tion completely decoupled from HAI-CC benchmarking. Consequently, no
existing benchmark jointly assesses fairness, deferral and complementarity
strategies, workload constraints, and multi-rater uncertainty, underscoring
the need for more comprehensive evaluation frameworks that reflect the re-
alities of clinical human-AI collaboration.

4. FairHAI Benchmark
In this section, we introduce FairHAI, a benchmark designed to jointly
evaluate AI fairness and HAI-CC using four public medical imaging datasets:
HAM10000 [83], CMMD [84], CheXpert [85], and MIMIC–CXR [86].
To
enable systematic comparison across competing methods, FairHAI incorpo-
rates simulated experts grounded in empirical evidence on the performance
gap between clinicians and AI systems [87]. The benchmark evaluates both
accuracy and fairness as functions of human involvement, allowing a unified
assessment of how collaborative decision-making impacts overall performance
and equity.
4.1. Datasets
To ensure consistency, we follow the preprocessing strategy, proposed
in[16], by binarising both sensitive attributes and classification labels.
HAM10000. The dataset consists of 9,948 dermatoscopic images across seven
diagnostic categories. Following [88], these are grouped into benign vs. malig-
nant classes. The sensitive attribute is Sex (Male/Female), enabling fairness
analysis across subgroups. The dataset includes 5,400 male images (4,492
benign, 908 malignant) and 4,548 female images (4,018 benign, 530 malig-
nant).

classes and Age (≤55 vs. >55) as the sensitive attribute. Malignant cases

4.2. Simulation of clinicians’ annotations to assess HAI-CC.
To enable systematic comparison across methods, FairHAI simulates clin-
icians’ annotations by assuming an error rate approximately 3% lower than
that of the Step 0 backbone AI model, consistent with empirical observations
of clinician-AI performance gaps in external validation [87]. Concretely, we
instantiate cohort-specific expert accuracies as follows: 98% for HAM10000,
95% for CheXpert, 95% for MIMIC–CXR, and, for CMMD, 92% for Group 1
(age ≤55) and 98% for Group 2 (age > 55). The injected errors follow a sym-
metric label noise model, i.e., labels are uniformly flipped among incorrect
classes according to the prescribed error probability, representing a standard,
analytically tractable assumption in noisy-label learning [89].
4.3. Evaluation Metrics
Binary classification performance is measured using AUC, which quanti-
fies how well a model separates positive from negative cases, while fairness
is assessed using Equity-Scaled AUC (ES-AUC) [82], which adjusts AUC to
penalise disparities in performance across demographic groups. Both metrics
are evaluated as functions of coverage, defined as the proportion of cases han-
dled exclusively by the AI system. In this setting, 100% coverage corresponds
to predictions made solely by the AI model, whereas 0% coverage reflects pre-
dictions made exclusively by clinicians. To capture overall behaviour across
coverage levels, we report the area under the AUC-coverage curve (AUACC)
and the area under the ES-AUC-coverage curve (AUESACC). Higher values
of these summary metrics indicate more favourable accuracy-coverage and
14


fairness-coverage trade-offs. Confidence intervals are computed using 2,000
bootstrap replicates, and statistical significance is evaluated via paired one-
sided t-tests.
4.4. Baselines
The simplest baseline is the standard Expected Risk Minimisation (ERM)
classifier, which trains a single model to maximise average accuracy without
considering fairness or human-AI interaction.
For the L2D setting, we report results for Dependent Cross-Entropy
(DCE) [90], a leading one-stage L2D method. We also include Fair L2D [14],
implemented by replacing the cohort-specific models with a single classifier
trained using cross-entropy loss alongside a fairness-regularised objective.
LECODU [81], which jointly models L2D and L2C, is also considered; it se-
lects a random cohort-specific model to combine with the simulated human
prediction or defers entirely to either the human or the model.
For AI fairness comparisons, we evaluate several state-of-the-art methods,
including GroupDRO [35], SWAD [36], FIS [82], and FairDi [91]. Because
these fairness-only baselines do not incorporate clinician collaboration, they
produce a single operating point at 100% coverage; to compute AUACC and
AUESACC, we pair this AI-only point with the human-only performance at
0% coverage. We also propose L2D-FairDi, a simple hybrid method that
combines L2D with FairDi by selecting either the Step 2 FairDi model or the
simulated expert for prediction.
5. Experiments
In this section, we first describe the training setup used for all models,
followed by the results of the FairHAI benchmark. We then analyse PecMan’s
deferral behaviour to cohort-specific models and clinicians, and conclude with
an ablation study evaluating the contribution of the cohort-specific models.

5.4. Ablation study on the cohort-specific models
We perform an ablation study on PecMan by replacing the multiple
cohort-specific models with a single fair model trained on a fairness method
(i.e., FairDi), referred to as L2D-FairDi. We evaluate both L2D-FairDi and
PecMan on HAM10000 and show the results in Fig. 7. In general, PecMan
outperforms L2D-FairDi on both cohort-specific (i.e., Figs. 7a and 7b) and
overall evaluation (i.e., Figs. 7c and 7d). Comparing L2D-FairDi (Fig. 7)
against standard L2D baselines (Fig. 5) demonstrates that using a fair back-
bone (e.g., FairDi) can also improve the performance of L2D.

6. Discussion and Conclusion
We presented PecMan, a unified framework that integrates AI fairness
with human-AI cooperation to improve patient equity and clinical efficacy.
Beyond the method, a key contribution of this work is FairHAI, a benchmark
that jointly evaluates accuracy, fairness, and human involvement across mul-

considerations. FairHAI fills an important gap left by prior benchmarks that
considered these dimensions in isolation, thereby accelerating progress in
equitable human-AI collaborative classification. Empirically, our proposed
PecMan surpasses methods that treat fairness or cooperation separately, de-
livering more balanced performance while supporting an efficient, clinically
viable workflow.
A current limitation of PecMan is the need to train cohort-specific mod-
els for each value of the sensitive attributes, which may become expensive as
the number of cohorts grows. This overhead could be mitigated by discover-
ing more efficient cohort structures, e.g., using hidden cohorts that capture
clinically meaningful strata without explicit demographic labels, reducing
the number of specialised models while preserving fairness and robustness
[12]. We envisage future work that couples PecMan with data-driven co-
hort discovery and active collaboration design, further strengthening equity,
reliability, and usability in real-world medical imaging deployments.

Abstract: Recent advances in data-centric medical AI have produced highly accurate diagnostic systems, but the emphasis on data curation and performance met- rics has not translated into widespread clinical adoption. We conjecture that this limited uptake stems from insufficient attention dedicated to the optimisation of fair performance across diverse patient populations and to workflow integration: performance biases can create regulatory barriers, and poorly integrated automation can disrupt clinical routines, degrade the qual- ity of human-AI collaboration, and reduce clinicians’ willingness to adopt AI tools. Prior work on workflow integration (e.g., Learning to Defer (L2D) and Learning to Complement (L2C)) and AI fairness has typically examined these challenges in isolation, overlooking their natural interdependence and the practical constraints of clinical environments, such as restricted clinician availability. We propose People-Centred Medical Image Analysis (PecMan), a human-AI framework that jointly optimises fairness, diagnostic accuracy, and workflow effectiveness through a dynamic gating mechanism that assigns cases to AI, clinicians, or both under clinician workload constraints. We also introduce the Fairness and Human-Centred AI (FairHAI) benchmark for evaluating trade-offs between accuracy, fairness, and clinician workload. Ex- periments using this benchmark show that PecMan consistently outperforms existing methods, paving the way for more trustworthy and clinically viable AI systems.
